title: Meta may use new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees
content:
Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts.
Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content.
As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta’s terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans.
“While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab,” the lab said.
Specifically, the updated terms say:
You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Notably, there is no mention of AI, but it’s inferred from a single use of the word “train” and references to automated scraping and crawling.

report.summary: Meta's updated commercial terms, effective October 30, force business accounts to permit automated crawling and AI training on their linked website content, with no opt-out.
report.background: AI companies increasingly need vast, fresh text to train and maintain models, and news publishers argue that scraping their archives without payment is copyright infringement. Several outlets, including The New York Times, have sued OpenAI over fair use, while others have signed lucrative licensing deals. Meta has faced its own scrutiny for scraping and for using public posts in AI training. Its new commercial terms, reported by Nieman Lab, shift the permission from social media posts to any website a business links in its Meta account. Because virtually every news organization operates at least one business page, the update gives Meta contractual consent to crawl and 'train' on publisher content, potentially sidestepping millions in licensing fees that outlets might otherwise charge and preempting the outcome of ongoing fair-use litigation.
key_points: The update takes effect October 30 and applies to all business accounts, from local shops to global publishers. There is no opt-out checkbox; Meta's terms essentially say that if a business disagrees, it should stop using Meta's services entirely. That removes the usual negotiating leverage publishers might use to demand payment for AI access.

The permission is broad. Business accounts must authorize Meta to use 'web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents' to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl any domains, web pages, or URLs linked to their products or services, and to pull updates periodically. That covers content far beyond a Facebook page.

Although the terms never say 'AI' directly, they permit Meta to use that content to 'develop, improve, research, train, and maintain' its products and services. Lawyers read 'train' and the scraping language as clear permission for AI training, making the clause a contractual workaround to copyright disputes.

News publishers are hit hardest. They could charge Meta millions annually to license article archives for AI training. Instead, the TOS would grant that access for free, undercutting the licensing market and weakening publishers' bargaining position in cases against OpenAI and others.

The move may set a precedent. If Meta's sweeping terms stand unchallenged, other large platforms could copy them, normalizing blanket AI-training consent buried in standard commercial agreements instead of negotiated licenses or court rulings on fair use. That shifts power further toward platforms that own distribution.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's terms show a new playbook: use platform dominance to obtain training data by contract rather than paying for licenses. That could lower data costs for Meta's models but push up legal and reputational risk, and invite regulator scrutiny over consent and fair competition. Developers building on or scraping the open web may face a more fragmented landscape of platform-specific terms, with some domains effectively enclosed. Smaller AI startups, lacking Meta's leverage, would still have to license or risk lawsuits. For regular users, content they publish or link through business accounts could be ingested into AI systems without meaningful notice or control, raising privacy and intellectual-property concerns. News consumers may see fewer original reporting resources if publishers lose a key revenue stream, though some outlets might retreat from Meta platforms, reducing the reach of local news.
report.tools: To monitor or resist AI crawling, watch the IETF AI Preferences (aipref) working group and the proposed ai.txt standard, plus robots.txt extensions. Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control and pay-per-crawl offer blocking and monetization; TollBit and ProRata provide licensing marketplaces; Spawning's Have I Been Trained lets creators check datasets. The open-source ai.robots.txt project from ai-robots-txt maintains lists of AI crawler user agents, while News/Media Alliance tracks policy developments.
